w: Two flights up a narrow staircase, Muddy Waters, Howlin Wolf, Bo Diddley and Etta James cut sides for Leonard and Phil Chess between 1957 and 1967. The Rolling Stones recorded an instrumental here in 1964 and named it after the street address. The Blues Heaven Foundation now runs tours through the same rooms.
s: Where Muddy Waters cut the blues electric
why: The Chicago studio where postwar electric blues was recorded and exported to the world.

w: Berry Gordy bought this modest house in 1959 with an 800 dollar family loan and built Studio A in the converted garage. Smokey Robinson, the Supremes, Marvin Gaye and the Jackson 5 all cut hits here before Motown decamped to Los Angeles in 1972. The control room and echo chamber survive exactly as they were.
s: Hitsville USA, birthplace of the Motown Sound
why: The garage studio that manufactured the Motown Sound and launched Motown's biggest stars.

w: Sam Phillips opened the Memphis Recording Service here in 1950 to capture blues and gospel no one else would record. Elvis Presley cut his first single in the same room, and Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, Jerry Lee Lewis and B.B. King all passed through. A 1956 jam among four of them was later dubbed the Million Dollar Quartet.
s: Birthplace of rock and roll on Union Avenue
why: The tiny studio where Sam Phillips recorded the sessions that launched rock and roll.

w: Four session players known as the Swampers left Rick Hall's Fame Studios in 1969 and opened their own room in a former coffin showroom on Jackson Highway. The Rolling Stones, Rod Stewart, Bob Seger and Paul Simon all came to this unglamorous stretch of Alabama chasing the loose, funky groove the house band laid down.
s: The Swampers cut soul in small-town Alabama
why: The unassuming Alabama studio whose house band defined the Muscle Shoals sound.

w: Built in 1892 as a revivalist tabernacle, the wooden pews and stained glass gave the Grand Ole Opry its home from 1943 to 1974. Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, Johnny Cash and Dolly Parton all made their Opry debuts under its arched roof, and the pin-drop acoustics still draw artists back to record live albums today.
s: The Mother Church of Country Music
why: The former gospel tabernacle that became country music's most revered stage.

w: Inside the Cecil Hotel on 118th Street, saxophonist and bandleader Henry Minton opened a club in 1938 where after-hours jam sessions let Thelonious Monk, Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker and Kenny Clarke tear apart swing tunes and rebuild them faster and stranger. Those late nights are widely credited with inventing bebop.
s: The Harlem club where bebop was born
why: The Harlem after-hours room where jam sessions forged bebop in the early 1940s.

w: A former art gallery in the French Quarter, Larry Borenstein let local musicians play for tip jars until the music outgrew the paintings. Allan and Sandra Jaffe took over in 1961, hiring elder musicians who had played alongside Buddy Bolden and Jelly Roll Morton, and built one of the only integrated stages in the Jim Crow South.
s: Traditional jazz kept alive since 1961
why: The bare-brick room that preserved and toured traditional New Orleans jazz worldwide.

w: Industrialist Hart Massey gave Toronto this 1894 concert hall, prized ever since for acoustics so precise a whisper carries to the back balcony. On May 15, 1953, it hosted the only recorded performance to unite Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Bud Powell, Charles Mingus and Max Roach, later released as The Greatest Jazz Concert Ever.
s: Where Parker, Gillespie and Mingus shared a stage
why: The 1894 hall that hosted jazz's only Parker-Gillespie-Mingus-Roach reunion.

w: A former coal yard became Mexico City's grandest dance hall in 1937, its sprung floor built for danzon, mambo and cha-cha-cha under low chandeliers. Perez Prado premiered Mambo No. 5 here in 1949, and dancers still arrive in vintage suits and dresses to move through the same steps their grandparents learned decades ago.
s: Danzon and mambo since 1937 in Colonia Guerrero
why: Mexico City's oldest surviving dance hall, where mambo had its 1949 premiere.

w: Behind an unmarked door on Riobamba, dancers have gathered since 1999 in a hall run on ritual: fixed tables, a strict cabeceo glance to invite a dance, and orchestras spanning tango's 1940s golden age. Locals call it the House of the Permanent Milonga, the only room said to schedule tango dancing every single day of the year.
s: Tango's house of the permanent milonga
why: The Buenos Aires milonga where tango's cabeceo etiquette runs uninterrupted daily.

w: Enslaved and freed Africans once carried salt up these stone steps in the old port district of Saude, and their descendants gathered here to sing and drum after dark. Samba pioneers Tia Ciata, Pixinguinha and Donga met on this rock to compose in the 1910s, and every Monday and Friday roda de samba circles still fill the same stairs.
s: The rock where samba was born
why: The stone stairway in Rio's old port where samba itself first took shape.

w: Clement Coxsone Dodd opened Jamaica's first Black-owned recording studio in 1963, and its house band cut the rhythm tracks that got recut and rerecorded across six decades of ska, rocksteady, reggae and dancehall. Bob Marley and the Wailers, Toots and the Maytals, Burning Spear and the Skatalites all began their recording careers within these walls.
s: The Motown of Jamaica on Brentford Road
why: The Kingston studio whose rhythms became the bedrock of Jamaican popular music.

w: Named for Bob Marley's nickname, itself borrowed from Rastafari founder Leonard Howell, Tuff Gong grew from the Wailers' 1970 label into a full complex with its own pressing plant, freeing Jamaican records from outside distributors. Marley, Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer all recorded here, and the studio still cuts tracks for his sons Damian and Ziggy.
s: Bob Marley's own label headquarters
why: The label and studio Bob Marley built to keep reggae's production in Jamaican hands.

w: A members-only social club in the Buenavista quarter hosted charangas and conjuntos through Havana's nightlife peak before the 1959 revolution shut such clubs down for good. Decades later producer Ry Cooder and Juan de Marcos Gonzalez borrowed its name for the aging musicians they reunited in 1996, turning a half-forgotten address into a global sensation.
s: The 1940s club that lent its name to a legend
why: The vanished Havana club whose name became shorthand for Cuban music's golden age.

w: Studio 2, a converted 1913 ballroom, sat close enough to the Berlin Wall that David Bowie could see East German guard towers from the control room window. He and producer Tony Visconti recorded Heroes here in 1977, reportedly inspired by watching Visconti kiss a backing singer in the Wall's shadow, and Iggy Pop's Lust for Life followed the same year.
s: Bowie wrote Heroes beside the Berlin Wall
why: The Kreuzberg studio by the Wall where Bowie recorded his Berlin Trilogy centerpiece.

w: Bjorn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson built Polar Studio in 1978 inside a converted cinema called Sportpalatset, modeling it on American rooms they had toured. ABBA recorded Voulez-Vous, Super Trouper and The Visitors here, and Led Zeppelin flew in to finish In Through the Out Door in the same rooms before the studio closed in 2004.
s: ABBA's private studio inside an old cinema
why: The purpose-built Stockholm studio ABBA designed for their own final three albums.

w: Factory Records and New Order sank the profits of Blue Monday into a cavernous former yacht showroom, opening it in 1982 with industrial decor years ahead of its time. Mike Pickering's Nude Night in 1988 turned the club into Britain's acid house ground zero, though it never escaped the debts and violence that forced its closure in 1997.
s: Factory Records' acid house palace
why: The Factory Records nightclub that midwifed British acid house and rave culture.

w: An abandoned 1930s public swimming pool outside Reykjavik sat empty until Sigur Ros bought it in 1999 and converted the pool hall into a recording room with a creek and pond visible through the control room windows. Every Sigur Ros album since the untitled 2002 record has been made here, alongside sessions for Damien Rice and Mugison.
s: Sigur Ros recorded inside a derelict pool
why: The disused Icelandic swimming pool Sigur Ros rebuilt into their home studio.

w: Danish architect Theophil Hansen modeled the Musikverein on a Greek temple when it opened in 1870, and its Golden Hall, lined with gilded caryatids beneath a mural of Apollo, is still ranked among the finest concert spaces on earth for its precise shoebox proportions. The Vienna Philharmonic has broadcast its New Year's Concert from this stage since 1939.
s: The Golden Hall's near-mythical acoustics
why: The 1870 Vienna hall whose acoustics have made it classical music's gold standard.

w: Fela Kuti turned his stage into a combined nightclub, shrine and political rally, and after Nigerian soldiers burned the original down in 1977 his children rebuilt it in Ikeja in 2000. Felabration fills the open-air venue every October, and Femi and Seun Kuti keep Afrobeat's horn-driven, hour-long grooves running most weekends of the year.
s: Where Fela Kuti's Afrobeat still plays nightly
why: The Lagos venue rebuilt by Fela Kuti's family to keep Afrobeat's home stage alive.

w: In the basement of the Ghion Hotel, Ethio-jazz pioneer Mulatu Astatke runs the club himself, mixing vibraphone-led instrumentals with Ethiopian scales he began developing after studying in London and New York in the 1960s. Communist-era crackdowns silenced Addis Ababa's jazz clubs for two decades before this room helped the scene revive.
s: Mulatu Astatke's own basement jazz club
why: The Addis Ababa club where Ethio-jazz's own founder still performs regularly.

w: One of a cluster of clubs, alongside the Vortex and the Goldfinger Lounge, that made District Six a cross-racial jazz hub through the 1950s and 60s, hosting saxophonists like Basil Coetzee and Winston Mankunku Ngozi who later defined the Cape jazz sound. Apartheid bulldozers razed the entire neighborhood by the mid-1970s, scattering its musicians into exile.
s: A jazz club erased with District Six
why: A jazz haunt from Cape Town's District Six, demolished under apartheid's forced removals.

w: Inside a 19th-century Nile-side palace on Roda Island, this museum holds the gowns, recordings and radio transcripts of Umm Kulthum, whose monthly Thursday-night concerts were broadcast live across the Arab world for over three decades. Cafes still empty out on the first Thursday of each month when Egyptian radio replays nothing but her voice.
s: The voice that stopped the Arab world monthly
why: The Cairo museum honoring the singer whose monthly broadcasts once halted a region.

w: Babylon opened in 1999 on a narrow Beyoglu backstreet before moving in 2015 into the vaulted halls of a 19th-century Ottoman beer factory in Bomonti. Sun Ra Arkestra, Patti Smith and Marianne Faithfull have all played its stage, and Downbeat magazine twice named it among the world's best jazz clubs despite its genre-hopping bookings.
s: An Ottoman brewery turned concert hall
why: Istanbul's boundary-pushing club, now housed inside a converted Ottoman brewery.

w: Sassoon House opened on the Bund in 1929 as the Cathay Hotel, its green pyramid roof a beacon for the treaty-port jazz age that made Shanghai the era's most cosmopolitan nightlife hub. The hotel's Old Jazz Band, formed in the 1980s from musicians who lived through that first golden age, still plays standards most nights in its ground-floor bar.
s: Octogenarians still swing on the Bund
why: The Bund hotel bar where Shanghai's jazz-age house band has played for decades.

w: Director Mehboob Khan built this seaside Bandra lot in 1954, and its five soundstages became the go-to shooting and recording location for Hindi cinema's most ambitious productions, including Mother India. Generations of playback singers and composers, from Lata Mangeshkar's sessions to R.D. Burman's arrangements, passed through its recording rooms.
s: The soundstage behind Bollywood's golden age
why: The Bandra film studio where much of Bollywood's classic-era sound was recorded.

w: A 20-year-old jazz fan named Mamoru Yoshida opened this Noge listening room in 1933 with a hundred 78s and a gramophone, inventing the jazz kissa format that later spread across postwar Japan. Wartime bombing destroyed the cafe and thousands of records, but Yoshida rebuilt it, and fans revived it again in 2012 after his death.
s: Japan's first jazz kissa, spinning since 1933
why: The Yokohama cafe that invented Japan's silent, high-fidelity jazz-listening culture.

w: Opened in Itaewon in 1976 as the country's very first dedicated jazz venue, All That Jazz became the training ground where nearly every prominent Korean jazz musician played early sets. Live music runs 364 nights a year, and though the club relocated to a sleeker Itaewon space in 2023, it remains the reference point for Seoul's jazz scene.
s: South Korea's first jazz club since 1976
why: The Itaewon club that has anchored South Korea's jazz scene for almost fifty years.
